📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered. FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations. Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

According to recent reports, “The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” noted Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”.

According to recent reports, “This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” mentioned FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

Industry observers note that “Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” noted Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” noted Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come.".

Examples of cases charged during this period include:.

Sources indicate that in the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses. Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted. In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo. His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

FBI’s Operation Steadfast Promise.

Industry observers note that operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a fresh FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI declared the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

Industry observers note that the FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

  • Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

Sources indicate that “Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”.

It has been revealed that “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”.

Industry observers note that according to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

It has been revealed that through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

Sources indicate that the jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

HHS-OIG and FBI investigated the case.

Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice declared the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

According to recent reports, the Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, presently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A. Kelly (who is emeritus in the English Department). It's called "Lawyers' Latin: Loquenda ut Vulgus?," and here's the introduction (though all 14 pages of the article are much worth reading):.

In "Rex v. Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A. P. Herbert's "Misleading Cases"), Mr. Wick, an advocate making his first appearance in the High Court, tries out his textbook Latin before the Lord Chief Justice. The young advocate, attempting to apply for a writ of certiorari, asks for "a rule of neesee of kairtiorahree." The Lord Chief Justice pretends not to understand this or any other of Mr. Wick's Latin phrases. When ultra vires is rendered ooltrah weerayze, the Court interrupts: "Stop! Listen, Mr. Wick. The two groups of sounds last formed by you have no meaning for me, and I order you not to make use of them again.".

Although the unfortunate Mr. Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:.

It is not for me at my time of life to learn a newly introduced language; it is not for the King's judges to remodel their diction according to the whims of pedagogues or the habits of the Junior Bar. The bitter conclusion is, Mr. Wick, that you must go away and learn to pronounce the Latin tongue correctly, according to the immemorial practice of your profession.

In a recent development, according to the juristic apophthegm, Loquendum ut vulgus, sentiendum ut docti, one should "speak like the common people but understand like the learned." When it comes to legal Latin, lawyers have observed the first part of this advice in various ways. Traditionally, Latin in England and other European countries has not been spoken uniformly but has been pronounced according to the sounds of the vernacular or lingua vulgaris of each region. Nowadays, however, most lawyers must be classed with the vulgus in never having learned Latin, and so they tend to avoid it whenever possible. But when an expression is unavoidable, they give it what they consider to be the "most common" pronunciation, or they imitate the commons in acting according to whim rather than according to rule. The result is what we might charitably call an eclectic or ad hoc approach—we hear, for example, ADD HOCK, ODD HAWK, ADD HOKE, ODD OAK, and so on.

Industry observers note that four different but internally consistent systems of Latin pronunciation have been used in England and America, each entirely "correct" and defensible in theory and in practice. The following analysis is concerned more with showing how the four methods have been adapted to English tongues than with reflecting how each would be spoken by a "native" or purist. My aim, after tracing the vagaries of Latin pronunciation, is to offer some practical recommendations to English-speaking lawyers using Latin phrases….

For the lawyer who occasionally uses Latin words or phrases, I recommend that all  expressions that have survived comfortably from an era when all Latin was pronounced in the English way—for example, et cetera—should continue to be pronounced as English, that is, in the English system of pronouncing Latin outlined above. But when Latin is cited as a foreign language, it should either be pronounced according to the system used by its author (if it is a literary citation) or according to any of the four systems outlined here that seems apt or convenient. Most often, no doubt, the system used will be the one learned in school.

Sources indicate that but lawyers and legal educators should keep in mind the certainty of Herbert's Lord Chief Justice that such "hateful sounds" as "ooltrah weerayze" (for ultra vires) "will never proceed from the lips of an English judge, however many innocent boys are instructed to make them at school." Those who learned the Classical system need to be cautioned against trying to impose it upon all Latin expressions as if it were the only correct, or the most correct, way of pronouncing Latin. To do so would be to mistake the purpose of the scholars who resurrected it. It was intended only for the classics of the Golden Age of Latin, not for later Latin or for technical Latin terms or phrases brought into the various vernaculars in modern times.

In a recent development, he labels the four methods "Classical (Ciceronian)," "Italian (Dantean)," "Continental (Chaucerian)," and "English (Shakespearean)," and discuss them further. He also cites a medieval source which I quite liked, at least with regard to pronunciation:.

[T]he desire to appear wise among the foolish … is itself a kind of madness.

Industry observers note that ian A. Brinksman, 42, of the District of Columbia was arrested following a search of his residence and charged by criminal complaint with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

Sources indicate that torres v. Carlson, currently pending before the Second Circuit, is a case brought by two Columbia University janitors under the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (KKK Act).

According to their complaint, masked individuals from Columbia University's anti-Israel alliance, armed with hammers, knives, bolt cutters, chains, and zip ties, stormed Columbia's Hamilton Hall and confronted the two men. The janitors' refusal to yield drew the ire of the rioters, who then assaulted them, detained them, and slurred them as Jew-lovers, Jew-workers, and Zionists. The rioters proceeded to seize the building, break windows to chain the doors shut, barricaded themselves inside, and unfurled banners declaring an "Intifada.".

Assuming the allegations are true, this seems like an open and shut case under the KKK Act, which the Supreme Court has described as reaching organized mob violence directed at a protected group and those perceived as standing with it. See Carpenters v. Scott, 463 U.S. 825 (1983).

Sources indicate that nevertheless, the district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. Covington & Burling has filed an amicus brief on behalf of Jon D. Michael of UCLA Law School, Matthew Segal of Tufts, with the Second Circuit, taking issue with the district court's decisions to:.

(1) resolve at the pleading stage questions of motive in the defendants' favor, crediting the defendants' characterization of their own motives over the plaintiffs' allegations and dismissing explicit antisemitic epithets as irrelevant;.

(2) treat supposed political motive as categorically negating discriminatory animus—disregarding both the mixed-motive framework that operates across federal antidiscrimination law and the settled principle that speech, even on political subjects, can evidence discriminatory intent; and,.

(3) view Jewish disagreement about whether all anti-Zionism is inherently antisemitic as dispositive proof that the specific anti-Zionist rhetoric in this case was not plausibly antisemitic—a standard that conflicts with binding precedent, contradicts how courts apply antidiscrimination law to groups other than Jews, and improperly gives any individual Jew the power to veto discrimination claims by all other Jews.

As an aside, there are several federal court decisions arising out of post-October 7 protest activity that strike many, including me, as applying stricter standards to civil rights plaintiffs claiming anti-Jewish violations of civil rights laws than precedent suggests applies to other plaintiffs.

No Pseudonymity for Woman Alleging She Was Falsely Accused of Sexual Relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, Doxed

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, from Doe v.
  • Jane Doe alleges four X (formerly Twitter) customers falsely accused her of having a sexual relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and doxxed her by posting on the social networking site her full name, employment and education history, phone numbers and addresses.
  • [A.] Parties to a lawsuit typically must identify themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, from Doe v. Doe (E.D. Pa.), decided today by Judge Gerald Pappert:.

Jane Doe alleges four X (formerly Twitter) customers falsely accused her of having a sexual relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and doxxed her by posting on the social networking site her full name, employment and education history, phone numbers and addresses. Doe asserts claims for defamation, false light, public disclosure of private facts and aiding and abetting. She seeks to proceed under a pseudonym because she fears for her safety, along with additional reputational and professional harm. The Court denies the motion because Doe's fear of harm does not outweigh the public's interest in open litigation.

[A.] Parties to a lawsuit typically must identify themselves. Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(a). In "exceptional cases," however, parties may proceed anonymously. To do so, "a plaintiff must show both (1) a fear of severe harm, and (2) that the fear of severe harm is reasonable." Courts balance multiple factors in considering whether to let someone proceed anonymously, including (1) the extent the identity of the litigant has been kept confidential; (2) the bases upon which disclosure is feared or sought to be avoided; (3) the public interest in maintaining the confidentiality of the litigant's identity; (4) whether the issue is purely legal in nature; (5) whether the party seeking to sue anonymously has illegitimate motives; and (6) the universal level of public interest in access to the identities of the litigants. The purpose of this balancing test "is to allow a district court to determine whether a litigant has a reasonable fear of severe harm that outweighs the public's interest in open litigation." ….

According to recent reports, the first factor "does not support anonymity where the litigant's identity has never been confidential." Doe has not kept her identity confidential. After Defendants doxxed her, by posting her picture, phone numbers and prior addresses, she publicly responded by "den[ying] the connection to Epstein in the thread of Defendants' posts.".

To establish fear of severe harm, Doe argues that "survivors and other named individuals have reported receiving death threats." Yet she does not allege how she will be threatened if forced to proceed under her real name, and courts reject "claims of harm or generalized fear that are found to be speculative and unsupported by evidence." As she notes, the Defendants have already shared her personal information with the public, so there is no greater risk if she proceeds under her own name.

According to recent reports, doe also alleges a "risk of reputational and professional devastation." But "[c]ourts in this Circuit do not recognize purely social and reputational harms, without more, as valid bases to prevail on this factor." Embarrassment or economic harm is not enough to justify proceeding anonymously either. And because her identity was made public, "litigating publicly will afford Doe the opportunity to clear [her] name" and "will not contribute further to the harm that [she] alleges has already occurred.".

In assessing the public's interest, courts consider whether "other similarly situated litigants [would] be deterred from litigating claims." Doe provides no reason to believe similarly situated litigants would be deterred from bringing defamation claims due to fear of disclosing their identities. The Epstein-related cases she relies upon involve plaintiffs who Epstein sexually assaulted, not individuals falsely accused of having a relationship with him.

If a plaintiff's claims are purely legal in nature, there is an "atypically weak public interest in knowing the litigant's identity." Doe's claims that Defendants falsely identified her as someone who had a sexual relationship with Epstein are inherently fact sensitive. For example, a key problem is whether Defendants "knew or were reckless about this falsity and had no good faith basis to claim that Plaintiff was the woman" identified in the Epstein files, and resolving that depends on the nature of the facts known to Defendants.

There is no evidence that Doe has illegitimate motives to proceed anonymously, which favors anonymity. The universal level of public interest in access to the identities of litigants, however, always weighs in favor of disclosing a plaintiff's identity.

The Court does not diminish the harm Doe claims to have suffered, but she has not established how using her real name would subject her to "severe harm," separate from what she has already allegedly endured from Defendants' past actions. Any harm she may suffer from using her own name is not outweighed by the "thumb on the scale that is the universal interest in favor of open judicial proceedings." ….

This is consistent, I think, with the cases generally holding that libel plaintiffs can't sue pseudonymously; see Roe v. Smith and the federal cases that it cites.

Latest Update: This Supreme Court "Deserves Our Celebration, Not Our Condemnation"

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Professor William Baude has an op-ed in the Fresh York Times, "This Is What an Independent, Competent Supreme Court Looks Like," defending the Supreme Court against its critics, left and right, and suggesting that many calls for court reform are misguided.
  • Noting that the Democratic electoral sweep has bolstered calls for reforming, and perhaps expanding, the Court to alter its course, Baude writes:.
  • Recent findings suggest that the left, understandably, strongly opposes the court's recent rulings on abortion, the Voting Rights Act, the unitary executive and so on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Professor William Baude has an op-ed in the Fresh York Times, "This Is What an Independent, Competent Supreme Court Looks Like," defending the Supreme Court against its critics, left and right, and suggesting that many calls for court reform are misguided.

Noting that the Democratic electoral sweep has bolstered calls for reforming, and perhaps expanding, the Court to alter its course, Baude writes:.

Recent findings suggest that the left, understandably, strongly opposes the court's recent rulings on abortion, the Voting Rights Act, the unitary executive and so on. These decisions are a big deal. But court reformers still suffer from a failure of perspective. If Chief Justice John Roberts could write an opinion essay, I would imagine him saying: "What? Ruling against the administration's misuse of the National Guard, sweeping emergency tariffs and attack on birthright citizenship, plus preserving the independence of the Federal Reserve and the integrity of the midterm elections, wasn't enough for you?".

In a recent development, the court has ruled against the administration in high-stakes cases on those issues all in the past year. And it has done so even though six of the justices were appointed by members of the president's party — three by President Trump himself. . . .

Under the circumstances of the second Trump term, the Supreme Court is doing amazingly well. If anything, it deserves our celebration, not our condemnation.

Indeed, the Court's conservatives, on the whole, have shown themselves more willing to constrain Trump's excesses than were the Court's liberals when faced with executive branch overreach by Presidents Biden or Obama.

Baude notes that the Court's willingness to reject Trump Administration priorities has caused some on the Right to question the conservative legal movement's commitment to originalism, and cautions that "what goes around comes around, and principles will be worth more in the long run." Of course, some conservatives' criticisms of the Court are for its failure to adhere to the principles some justices espouse (including originalism), not that those principles are getting in the way of making America great again.

On the question of judicial reform, Baude strikes a cautionary note, particularly if court reform is nothing more than an effort to reverse the Court's current trajectory.

In the abstract, there is nothing wrong with bipartisan judicial reform. The Supreme Court should not be preserved in amber. But partisan judicial reform — reform motivated by frustration with specific judicial decisions and the hope that the reformed court will rule differently — is a dangerous game. Because partisan reform is a tactic equally available to both sides, it accomplishes little in the long run except to accelerate the court's transformation into a political superweapon. Such a tactic might be a short-run necessity in extreme circumstances, but we are far from those extremes.

According to recent reports, he also--quite correctly--calls out the obsession with judicial ethics as "superficial." He could add that such concerns are nearly always one-sided and selective. While it may be appropriate to further limit the justices' outside income or ability to accept gifts, we should not pretend that any such reforms would have any effect on the Court's decisions.

According to recent reports, the justices' views on big issues are well formed. The justices themselves aren't for sale; book income reflects their increasing celebrity, not any specific quid pro quo. To be sure, it is quite possible that travel and gifts and book sales subtly reinforce the justices' incentives to play to their respective fan bases. But this kind of corruption is quite indirect, and at the same time comes from so much more than money. So ethics reform is unlikely to change much about what the court actually does.

In the end, Baude thinks the best argument for court reform is as a placebo: To convince the public that something has been done so that attention can turn to more pressing concerns. As he concludes this point: "If pointless reforms cause many Americans to believe that the court is better — more independent, less corrupt and so on — that would be great for the country.".

Industry observers note that I largely agree with Baude's piece, though I may be more open to certain sorts of reforms than he reveals in this piece. Reforms that represent genuine political engagement with the work of the courts, such as measures to alter or channel jurisdiction could be quite beneficial. Measures to reduce backlogs, limit forum shopping, constrain unwarranted or overly expansive equitable relief, and expand the Court's mandatory jurisdiction are all worth considering. They also represent the sort of meaningful legislation that Congress should engage in--legislation that requires Congress to take seriously its constitutional responsibilities. (In this regard, I view the willingness to engage with jurisdictional questions in the pending infrastructure reform bill to be a welcome sign, even if I might not endorse every jurisdictional measure the bill contains.).

As Baude ends his essay, courts are not above criticism, and this includes the Supreme Court. It is nonetheless is vital to distinguish between criticisms of how the Court operates and performs its job from substantive or ideological disagreement with the decisions the Court reaches.

"Let the celebrations at my fan clubs in the City of Berkeley begin," Yoo stated in an email. "Great as our university is, it would not allow a school to focus on restoring the central importance of western civilization to the education of all undergraduates." . . .

"I am sorry, however, that my departure will reduce the number of conservative professors in public law at Berkeley by 100 percent," Yoo stated in the email. "I hope that the university will take this as an opportunity to consider that the notion of diversity should, most importantly, include ideology, not just the usual race, gender, and economic categories that my colleagues usually mean by diversity.".

There had been one other right-leaning law professor at Berkeley, our co-blogger Orin Kerr, but he left Berkeley for Stanford in 2025.

According to Dean of Berkeley Law Erwin Chemerinsky, Yoo's decision to leave the faculty was entirely his own.

"John (Yoo) has been an notable part of the faculty for many years," Chemerinsky noted in an email. "This was entirely John's decision to retire. … He has indicated to me for a few years his thoughts about retiring. John is a very successful teacher and an eminent scholar." . . .

Yoo's move is also less drastic than it might appear, as he is moving from one blue state to another. All of the other California transplants that have moved to Austin helped make sure of that (with a major assist from the Republican Party).

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” mentioned Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”.

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

Recent findings suggest that in late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI Newly introduced York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of Latest York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

I really wanted to attend the FHB Summit work this year, but it was my daughter’s birthday (which was epic), and my wife Megan had just gotten back from a work trip. Anyway..just dropping a line.

Cheers, Will Bown www.turnkeybuildersvt.com.

I meant to send this story a bit ago when you were discussing those scary old Milwaukee right-angle drills. Mike really knocked it out of the park with his story about a person spinning under a truck. My story is on par, though I didn’t see it first hand.

An electrician I worked with had a right-angle drill mishap that stands out as one of the greatest, mostly harmless construction stories I’ve heard. He was standing on an upside-down bucket reaching and drilling upward into the ceiling area with a right-angle drill. You see where this is going, right?

Sources indicate that the drill stuck on something, kicked back, and it twisted him off of the bucket. When the bucket tipped he was left hanging by the drill and holding onto the trigger. He spun, dangling in the air, until the cord wrapped around him enough to unplug itself. If I remember correctly, his partner had to help extract him from the situation.

I sold my right-angle drill to an electrician recently because I hadn’t used it in 10 years due to fear of injury. That was the scariest tool in my carpentry arsenal, not the spinning blade tools.

To the disembodied voices telling me to buy more tools,.

Recent findings suggest that are active radon mitigation systems creating radon mines? Does constant suction create defined pathways for more nearby radon to escape the ground? In my 1946 Pleasant Grove, Utah, house I have a partially completed radon mitigation system. It is at the moment just sucking air from the unencapsulated crawlspace. I’m actively monitoring radon level, and they stay below the 4 picocuries-per-liter threshold while the fan is on.

Recent findings suggest that I turned the radon fan off temporarily. When I finally noticed the radon levels creeping back up, they were much higher than ever before (including before installing the fan). That’s what made me wonder about this idea of creating an easier channel for the radon.

I’m renovating an entire house in Rochester, New York, and have an insulation question about the ceiling of a mid-1980s addition.

Industry observers note that when I bought the house, the ceiling had Sheetrock with significant sags between the 24-in.-o.c. framing, including one much wider sag in a single bay. I removed the Sheetrock and found the ceiling cavities packed tightly with cellulose, which was weighing down very stretched-out poly sheeting. I also found a roughly 42-in. span with no framing (related to old skylights, I believe). I’ve since had all the cellulose removed and am starting fresh.

The roof is a vented assembly with a ridge vent and several soffit vents on each side, but there were no rafter/insulation baffles. I’m wondering whether there was ever meaningful soffit-to-ridge airflow through the roof cavities.

Industry observers note that the existing roof sheathing is also in mediocre condition. There aren’t active leaks, but I expect to replace the sheathing when I redo the roof down the road.

That leads me to a few questions:.

I’ve attached a Google Drive folder with photos that should illustrate the situation: https://photos.app.goo.gl/TGeTmNWneBXaFhpi7.

Thanks in advance, and I love the pod!

Noah Kanter Nth Degree Painting.

Latest Update: Why Exactly Does The Supreme Court "Deserve Our Celebration"?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that will Baude has a latest essay in the New York Times titled, "This Is What an Independent, Competent Supreme Court Looks Like." The graphic depicts a giant judge standing boldly with people on the left and right tugging at his robe in either direction.
  • The left, understandably, strongly opposes the court's recent rulings on abortion, the Voting Rights Act, the unitary executive and so on.
  • The court has ruled against the administration in high-stakes cases on those issues all in the past year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that will Baude has a latest essay in the New York Times titled, "This Is What an Independent, Competent Supreme Court Looks Like." The graphic depicts a giant judge standing boldly with people on the left and right tugging at his robe in either direction. The face of the giant judge does not resemble any current member of the Court, but it may as well be Chief Justice Roberts. You see, Baude urges us to celebrate the Court because of its independence, but the only data he adduces to demonstrate that independence is that the Court's conservatives rule against President Trump:.

The left, understandably, strongly opposes the court's recent rulings on abortion, the Voting Rights Act, the unitary executive and so on. These decisions are a big deal. But court reformers still suffer from a failure of perspective. If Chief Justice John Roberts could write an opinion essay, I would imagine him saying: "What? Ruling against the administration's misuse of the National Guard, sweeping emergency tariffs and attack on birthright citizenship, plus preserving the independence of the Federal Reserve and the integrity of the midterm elections, wasn't enough for you?".

The court has ruled against the administration in high-stakes cases on those issues all in the past year. And it has done so even though six of the justices were appointed by members of the president's party — three by President Trump himself. . . .

Recent findings suggest that under the circumstances of the second Trump term, the Supreme Court is doing amazingly well. If anything, it deserves our celebration, not our condemnation.

There are many, many problems with this approach.

Let's start with the two most conservative members of the Court, Justices Alito and Thomas. They ruled for President Trump in all the cases Baude mentions: the National Guard, tariffs, birthright citizenship, the Federal Reserve, and various election cases. Do their votes cut against the image of an independent Court? They owe Trump nothing, and had the backbone to resist retiring and giving Trump two more picks. (The same cannot be mentioned for Justice Breyer's "independence" from President Biden.).

It has been revealed that moreover, in each of those cases, one or more of the Trump appointees was in dissent with Alito and Thomas: Gorsuch dissented in Trump v. Illinois, Kavanaugh dissented in Learning Resources v. Trump, Gorsuch dissented in Trump v. Barbara, Gorsuch and Barrett dissented in Trump v. Cook, and so on. Did these Trump appointees not demonstrate independence in these cases? Or, should their votes against Trump in other cases balance out their votes for Trump in these cases?

According to recent reports, justice Kagan made this point expressly during her remarks at the Ninth Circuit Judicial Conference. She mentioned that the Court "has checked the executive branch" in "very significant cases." In these cases, Kagan explained, "it's the chief justice with a little bit of a floating cast of characters around him." Truly, she views Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett as an interchangeable "floating cast of characters." The liberals (almost) aways vote in lockstep, but a conservative vote is always up for grabs. Tell us how you really feel, Elena. (I'll have much more to say about Kagan's comments at Catholic University in my next Civitas column.).

Sources indicate that baude jokes about the Chief Justice writing an opinion essay for all the cases where he wrote the majority opinion ruling against Trump. But reality is stranger than fiction. The truth is John Roberts writes opinion essays every term. Everything he says and does is designed to maintain some faux equilibrium. He even bundles together some essays (Slaughter and Cook) to maximize press coverage. The better question is what would Justices Thomas and Alito write if they were untethered?

The measure of independence cannot be how often Trump loses. Justices Thomas and Alito argue in those cases that the law actually supports Trump. They would contend (I think) that their colleagues' lack of independence explain their votes. Or, as Justice Alito writes in his newly introduced book, they are "insecure originalists.".

It has been revealed that baude's essay also suffers from a tragic case of bothesidesism. He tries very, very hard to cast aspersion on the right as well as the left.

Sources indicate that with their sweeping midterm victory, Democrats are exploring ideas for a package of reforms to the Supreme Court. And it's not just Democrats: In recent months, the court has managed to invite calls for reform from both sides of the aisle. Some conservatives are even willing to discuss expanding the number of justices.

On the left, presidential candidates and elected members of Congress have called for Court expansion. On the right, members of the House and Senate introduced a constitutional amendment to fix the size of the Court at 9. Which conservatives called for Court expansion? Other than some MAGA posters, I can't think of anyone relevant.

Sources indicate that some on the right see these decisions as betrayals. But the right-wing critics fail to possess patience or to understand constitutional principle. Conservative legal thinkers spent two generations rightly emphasizing the importance of originalist interpretation and limited government. And while some on the right want to move away from these principles now that they can frustrate right-wing rule, what goes around comes around, and principles will be worth more in the long run.

It is pretty clear Baude is talking about Trump who has posted on X about how his appointees betrayed him. Shame on President Trump for not possessing the patience of a life-tenured law professor and failing to read the latest issue of the Harvard Law Review. Come on. Trump is a politician who has two years left in office. His time horizon and expectations are different from academics. The problem, of course, is that Thomas and Alito insist that originalist principles support the President. It is Chief Justice Roberts, the Judge Hercules in Baude's World, who eschews any sort of originalist jurisprudence.

Sources indicate that baude continues to point out problems with the Court. These are all liberal complaints. Everything he states may as well be taken from the Strict Scrutiny podcast:.

This is not to say that the court is doing perfectly well. It has plenty of problems. The justices face many hard cases, and they are subject to human temptations. They also struggle with the exercise of discretion in the when and how of their rulings, which can seem arbitrary or overly manipulative. These struggles are especially apparent in the court's inconsistent treatment of precedents, in its decisions about which cases to take in the first place and in the many controversies over its "shadow docket" (or interim orders docket, if you prefer).

Recent findings suggest that does Baude see any problem with decisions like Obergefell which overruled millenia of precedent to invent a constitutional right without any basis in original meaning? Did that ruling justify "court reform"?

In the end, Baude mentions almost under his breath that "modest Court reform" might include "term limits.".

There is one good argument for court reform: If anything, it might have only a placebo effect — it would be a fake medicine, causing some people to feel cured and convincing the public that all of the problems they ascribe to the court have been solved. A few more modest court reforms, such as gift caps or even term limits, may well be mostly harmless. If pointless reforms cause many Americans to believe that the court is better — more independent, less corrupt and so on — that would be great for the country.

In a recent development, baude does not tell us whether term limits require a constitutional amendment, or if they can be imposed by statute. I suspect this passage will be the main sentence from Baude's essay that people end up citing. To call term limits "modest" gives the whole game away. Baude indicates Term limits would make America great again!

Recent findings suggest that here is my bottom line. I would rather that the current crop of Justices fearlessly follow the meaning of the Constitution, results be damned, then feign "independence" as a means to avoid "Court Reform." What is the consolation prize for faking independence? Baude offers that term limits would be "harmless," basically a placebo, to help the body politic. With friends like these, who needs enemies? Judges cannot control what politicians do. They should not try to play a game.

It would not surprise me if Chief Justice Roberts retires when a Democrat is President to permanently bolster his reputation for independence. Progressives and their allies would place Roberts in the Judicial Parthenon alongside John Marshall and others. But John Glover is still not fooling anyone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

According to recent reports, as part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” stated Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”.

In a recent development, “By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” remarked U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”.

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution. We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”.

Industry observers note that “The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”.

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

#113150. Tech Report: Two Cheers for the Supreme Court - Though Not More

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Two Cheers for the Supreme Court - Though Not More

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In  a much-discussed recent Latest York Times article, University of Chicago law Prof.
  • With their sweeping midterm victory, Democrats are exploring ideas for a package of reforms to the Supreme Court.
  • Recent findings suggest that still, these calls do not reflect a bipartisan agreement on what is wrong with the court.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In  a much-discussed recent Latest York Times article, University of Chicago law Prof. (and former VC blogger) Will Baude praises the Supreme Court and its independence:.

With their sweeping midterm victory, Democrats are exploring ideas for a package of reforms to the Supreme Court. And it's not just Democrats: In recent months, the court has managed to invite calls for reform from both sides of the aisle. Some conservatives are even willing to discuss expanding the number of justices.

Recent findings suggest that still, these calls do not reflect a bipartisan agreement on what is wrong with the court. The calls for reform simply reflect the fact that the court has managed to offend people on the left and right. Defying the Trump administration on key agenda items while also enforcing colorblindness and overruling Roe v. Wade has left it with few true fans.

Industry observers note that the left, understandably, strongly opposes the court's recent rulings on abortion, the Voting Rights Act, the unitary executive and so on. These decisions are a big deal. But court reformers still suffer from a failure of perspective. If Chief Justice John Roberts could write an opinion essay, I would imagine him saying: "What? Ruling against the administration's misuse of the National Guard, sweeping emergency tariffs and attack on birthright citizenship, plus preserving the independence of the Federal Reserve and the integrity of the midterm elections, wasn't enough for you?".

The court has ruled against the administration in high-stakes cases on those challenges all in the past year. And it has done so even though six of the justices were appointed by members of the president's party — three by President Trump himself….

In a recent development, under the circumstances of the second Trump term, the Supreme Court is doing amazingly well. If anything, it deserves our celebration, not our condemnation.

Sources indicate that I agree with much of this. I made similar points in two articles critiquing proposals for court-packing (see here and here), emphasizing the importance of the Court's rulings against Trump, and how they were not simple gimmes. In each case, there were at least minimally plausible arguments the other way, such that a Court intent on helping Trump and the GOP at all costs could have found a way to do it:.

Industry observers note that over the last 18 months, the Supreme Court has played a key role in thwarting several major Trump power grabs. The most recent example is the birthright citizenship case, which prevented him from stripping citizen status from hundreds of thousands of children of undocumented migrants and temporary visa holders, thereby subjecting them to potential deportation.

In a recent development, in Learning Resources v. Trump (which I helped litigate), the court struck down Trump's attempt to use the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose the highest tariff schedule since the Hoover-era Smoot-Hawley tariffs that notoriously exacerbated the Great Depression. Trump's tariffs would have imposed some $1.7 trillion of new taxes on Americans. The court's reasoning was not limited to the specifics of IEEPA. All six justices in the majority made clear that they rejected the notion that the president could have a virtually unlimited power to impose tariffs. Thus, the precedent is likely to help block his efforts to twist other statutes into authorization for unconstrained presidential tariff authority….

In lesser-known cases, the court blocked Trump's effort to use the National Guard against blue states (thereby causing him to abandon the effort) and twice used brief "shadow docket" decisions to block deportations under the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 and signal that courts could review Trump's invocation of that law….

[Some critics] acknowledg… these second-term defeats are real yet insist… that they are just "a floor." But protecting people from massive power grabs that gravely endangered the liberty and well-being of millions is no small matter. The same goes for blocking executive use of the military to suppress domestic opposition. And, in each of these cases, the Trump administration had at least minimally plausible arguments for their positions, sometimes backed by prominent conservative legal scholars and commentators. A court inclined to give Trump and the GOP whatever they want could easily have gone the other way on some or all of them. Even if the court could and should have done more to constrain Trump, these rulings are crucial safeguards for liberty and democracy.

It has been revealed that unlike Josh Blackman, I think the conservative justices' willingness to rule against Trump and GOP priorities is a notable measure of their independence. It's a strong sign that they are not simply partisan hacks, and not beholden to any president or party. That doesn't prove that any time a conservative judge rules against a Republican president, they are necessarily right to do so. Being independent and being right are not the same thing. But both are important.

According to recent reports, at the same time, I am less of a fan of the current Supreme Court majority than Will Baude is. In my view, they have made several very bad decisions:.

Still, it is true that the conservative majority has issued some very bad rulings. I agree with Craig that Trump v. United States—the 2024 presidential immunity ruling—is one of them. But that decision does not give the president blanket immunity from all criminal prosecution for actions taken while in office or even categorical immunity for all "official acts." It's a bad decision but not one that totally eliminates criminal prosecution as a check on presidential abuses of power…. [I also have ambivalent views on Trump v. Slaughter and Louisiana v. Callais].

In my view, the Roberts Court has made several decisions that are worse than any of the above. Most notable are Trump v. Hawaii, the awful 2018 anti-Muslim "travel ban" case, and the similar recent decision in Mullin v. Doe, the Haitian TPS case. In both of these cases, the court's conservative justices turned a blind eye to blatantly unconstitutional discrimination in the immigration context (in one case based on religion, in the other on race). This is part of the court's broader pattern of indefensible double standards when it comes to immigration restrictions.

On top of that, the Roberts Court recently gave us the Supreme Court's worst Takings Clause ruling in many years, undermining its previously generally good record on constitutional property rights.

Recent findings suggest that thus, I am only willing to offer two cheers for the Court. To earn three, the justices would need to give us fewer stinkers!

In a recent development, that said, the Court's record in checking Trump should give pause to advocates of court-packing and other "reform" measures that would have the effect of destroying judicial review. As explained more fully in my two recent articles critiquing court-packing (here and here) the proper baseline of comparison is not an ideal Supreme Court, but one that would have little or no ability to check the party in power, especially if that party controls both the White House and Congress. The latter is the likely result of court-packing. By that standard, the Roberts Court has had a massive beneficial impact. Between them, the birthright citizenship, tariff, and National Guard decisions have saved millions of people from severe threats to their livelihoods and civil liberties (most notably hundreds of thousands of children saved from potential deportation under Trump's birthright citizenship executive order).

It has been revealed that like Baude, I am not opposed to all possible Supreme Court reforms. For example, I am a long-time supporter of Supreme Court term limits. I am also open to imposing tighter ethics constraints on the justices, and have criticized Justice Alito's claim that Congress lacks power to regulate the Court on such matters. Again, like Baude, I highly doubt that ethics reforms would have any significant impact on the Court's rulings. But it may still be desirable to constrain outside gifts and the like, if only to prevent more serious ethics complications from potentially arising in the future.

I also think some proposals to better manage and constrain the "shadow docket" may be desirable, though I will not try to cover this difficult concern here.

Finally, Baude is right that the Court's relative unpopularity is a potential danger. It is, as he suggests, caught between progressives who believe it's way too conservative, and right-wingers who blame it for constraining Trump too much.

Industry observers note that at the same time, it's worth remembering that the Supreme Court is less unpopular than either of the other branches of government, and that most of its major recent decisions enjoy majority public support. As I always emphasize, a decision's popularity is far from a good indication of its correctness. But such (relative) popularity can potentially protect the Court against political attack.

Sources indicate that finally, I would note this: As prominent conservative legal commentator Ed Whelan points out, the results of the recent midterm election make it highly likely that Justice Alito, Justice Thomas, or both will ultimately be replaced by a liberal Democratic nominee. Democrats considering court-packing should ask themselves whether they really rather destroy judicial review, or see it wielded by what may well soon be a liberal court.

For my part, I have plenty of differences with the current conservative majority. And if it is replaced by a more liberal one, I expect to have many disagreements with that majority, as well. But either is far preferable to just getting rid of judicial review entirely. The Trump era has provided plenty of additional evidence for that proposition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

According to recent reports, according to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private organization that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other owners to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

In a recent development, the FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Industry observers note that trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

It has been revealed that an indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell. Gases like radon and carbon monoxide are colorless and odorless but dangerous if inhaled, and these home devices may also identify other pollutants, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and airborne particulate matter like dust and pollen. They can serve as a first alert, signaling when to leave an area where the air is unsafe or prompting you to start clearing pollutants and head off health problems. Keep in mind, however, that not all air quality monitors detect all harmful pollutants.

In a recent development, concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors. We began by extensively researching more than 40 air quality monitors to narrow the field and then selected a range of models to test. (Spoiler: Not all of the air quality monitors we tested earned a spot on this lineup.).

It’s easy to take steps to improve the air quality in your home with an air quality monitor. The best air quality monitor will depend on which pollutants you want to keep track of and whether you prefer a basic or tech-forward model. Our favorite is the Airthings 292 Wave Mini Indoor Air Quality Monitor. It monitors total VOCs (TVOCs), radon, temperature, humidity, mold risk, and outdoor pollen levels. It also comes with smart-home capability and easy-to-use air quality indicators, and it’s suitable for multi-room use.

Ahead, find out what the devices can do and see how the models listed below fared in our hands-on testing to help you choose the best air quality monitor for your home.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air quality monitor depends on specific needs, from detecting VOCs to integrating with smart-home systems.

According to recent reports, when it comes to air quality monitors, accuracy is essential. While we didn’t have access to a laboratory for testing, we could offer a measure of control by testing all the monitors under similar situations to see if the readings would correspond when compared to one another. The following monitors all detected the presence of pollutants in our hands-on tests, and we would not hesitate to recommend any of them to help our readers choose a product to detect airborne pollutants in the home.

To measure chemical pollutants in the air without spending a lot, consider the well-priced Wave Mini. The Wave Mini detects TVOCs, humidity, and temperature in the room. After spending a few hours exposed to a dish of oil-based stain in a closed box, the monitor’s TVOC levels spiked. When we compared its temperature and humidity readings to other monitors being tested, the readings were comparable. We believe it accurately portrayed all three readings.

It has been revealed that the Wave Mini offers visual indication of air quality in the room, which is accessible when the user waves a hand in front of the monitor. A light flashes green for “healthy,” yellow for “caution,” and red for “poor” air quality.

Industry observers note that people can purchase a hub separately, allowing them to integrate with smart-home products such as Google Assistant and Alexa. The Wave Mini also tracks outdoor pollen levels via the app that syncs with a local weather service. If users don’t have a specific need for monitoring carbon monoxide, radon, or dust, the Wave Mini may be just the right budget-friendly device to keep track of chemical pollutants in the home.

Get the Airthings 292 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Amazon, increasingly offering more of its own brand of products, has entered the air quality monitor field with this device, which measures particulate matter, TVOCs, carbon monoxide, humidity, and temperature. It’s ideal for bedrooms because the small white cube with a little stainless steel vent in front doesn’t have a large display that might keep some folks awake. Instead, a tiny indicator light at the top that shines green, yellow, or red notifies the user of the current air quality. We didn’t find the indicator light to be bright enough to be annoying; it was just bright enough to display the air quality at a glance. However, it only works in a darkened room—it’s not bright enough to see it in sunny daylight.

It has been revealed that the Amazon smart air quality monitor syncs with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and we found it simple to connect to both. We were unable, however, to connect the monitor to our Echo Show (not included), although it’s advertised as being able to do so. We’re not sure what caused the glitch, since our Echo Show and the monitor individually synced with the Alexa app, but it’s possible it will only connect with newer models of the Echo Show (ours is an older model). Still, the Alexa app on our smartphone provided excellent real-time readings and charts that made it easy to see the air quality.

We tested this monitor in our test box for VOCs and particulate matter. For the first test, we put a dish of oil-based stain in the box, gave it a couple of hours to infiltrate the air, and then checked the app. The VOC reading had spiked. We then opened the box to check the monitor—the indicator light shone red (hazardous air quality). For the second test, we shook the dust mop over the box and monitored the app on our phone. The PM2.5 reading spiked in about 5 minutes and fell 20 minutes later as the dust settled.

According to recent reports, to test the CO sensor, we put the monitor in the garage, started the car, and closed the doors. We watched on our smartphone as the CO reading on the app rose. When we opened the garage door, the indicator light was red. We brought the monitor out into the fresh air, and the light turned green in about 10 minutes.

According to recent reports, compared with the other monitors we tested, the Amazon smart air quality monitor’s temperature and humidity readings were right on target. Overall, we liked this little monitor, and we felt it was accurate and discreet enough not to detract from bedroom or nursery decor.

Get the Amazon air quality monitor at Amazon.

This monitor was quite an overachiever in our testing! It connects using Bluetooth technology via the Airthings app and provided detailed reports about our home’s air quality. It will also connect to smart-home devices, such as Alexa, but not via Wi-Fi. Instead, users must download the IFTTT app for their smartphone, which allows a connection between Wave Plus and Alexa.

The first test we performed on the Wave Plus was in a friend’s home where radon was previously detected and is being treated. They have a professional radon detector, so we wanted to see if the Wave Plus would also detect the gas. We positioned it in the basement of the home and left it there for a week.

On our return, we checked the Airthings app and found a radon reading of 3.5pCi/L. This was the exact reading the professional radon detector was showing. When we waved a hand in front of the Wave Plus, it flashed a yellow light that told us the air quality was affected but not hazardous. When we took the Wave Plus outside in the fresh air, the radon level dropped, and the light turned green to indicate healthy air.

Recent findings suggest that we then tested the Wave Plus in our test box where we exposed it for 2 hours to a dish of oil-based stain, a product that contains VOCs. Before we chose monitors for hands-on testing, we researched more than 40 models, looking for various sensor types and paying close attention to buyers’ reviews and ratings.
